events.excerpt: AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC. As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.” The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs. “You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use. AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.” The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub . The Register found over 1,300 items on that page. While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud. “It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.”
events.headline: AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC

events.excerpt: The Statistical Reality of Coding Agents For technical decision-makers, leaderboard order can look more conclusive than the underlying comparisons allow. The ExpertCrowd-SWE study , an author-reported coding-agent benchmark submitted on November 9, 2026, provides a nuanced look at seven frontier coding agents. Rather than a simple ranking, the study identifies four statistical tiers, highlighting where evidence separates models and where it remains inconclusive. Four tiers, not seven distinct places The paper evaluated seven models on 100 expert-authored software-engineering tasks drawn from 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. Each model attempted each task five times. The paper reports 3,495 scored runs. Gemini 3.8 Flash had no valid run on one assigned task, so its score covers 99 tasks. The reported averages are: Opus 5.5 (67.3%), GPT-6 Astra (63.7%), Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0% across 99 tasks), Qwen 3.8 Max (33.5%), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (32.5%), and Grok 4.6 (32.2%). These averages form a four-tier pattern. The bottom three models—Qwen, DeepSeek, and Grok—are not statistically separated from one another in pairwise comparisons. events.excerpt: Russian cloud operator Yandex has admitted to data loss after a drone attack on one of its datacenters. The attack, which Ukrainian press said was ordered by Kyiv, happened in early October and caused a fire and subsequent outage at Yandex’s ru-central1-b availability zone. Subsequent strikes targeted more Yandex datacenters and disrupted more of the company’s cloud and payment services. On Tuesday, Yandex posted an update on its recovery efforts, which it spun as something of a triumph because it restored over 97 percent of customer data. Of course that also means the company lost 2.84 percent of customer data, which it blamed on “critical hardware damage and a lack of backups on the platform.” It’s unclear if Yandex’s use of the phrase “on the platform” indicates it doesn’t keep backups of its own cloud, if whatever resilience techniques it employs don’t create multiple copies of customer data, or if clients didn’t protect their data. Whatever happened, Yandex has decided to enable backups by default for all VMs customers create in its cloud. That decision will mean customers will consume and pay for more Yandex resources, unless they opt out of the automated backups. events.excerpt: I never think much about buoys unless I’m watching a movie about man-eating sharks. But it turns out they don’t just float out on there on the ocean for the nice aesthetics; they’re there for a reason. Wave buoys, for instance, are there primarily to measure wave activity. And like everything else these days, the information they provide is available online. TheMaritimePilot used that data to build this desktop model that mirrors the movement of a selected real-life buoy . TheMaritimePilot happens to be a maritime pilot in Belgium, so his work relies on the data provided by wave buoys. So, this idea makes perfect sense for him. But I think everyone else will appreciate it, too. This is called SeaGlance and it is a small buoy, a few inches tall, that bounces around on virtual waves rolling across a desk. Of course, there aren’t any actual waves and so the buoy actually rides from a series of cables. Eight stepper motors can pool those cables in and out, moving the buoy up and down — and even tilting it side-to-side. SeaGlance turns those motors according to live data that it fetches over Wi-Fi. SeaGlance can grab data from a variety of different sources. Many of them are country-specific and provided by those country’s relevant agencies, but they’re usually freely available to eve
events.headline: This Actuated Desktop Model Mirrors the Movement of a Real-Life Buoy

events.excerpt: A microphone is an odd — and somewhat disturbing — thing to find inside a coffee machine. That's what caught the attention of hardware hacker Robin M., who spotted one mentioned in the service documentation for a Spengler PSL50. What started as an attempt to figure out why it was there quickly turned into a much bigger hardware hacking project involving embedded Linux, an unsecured debug interface, a questionable USB update system, and, of course, Doom . According to the machine's supplier, the microphone was intended for future presence detection and accessibility features, but wasn't actually being used. Further investigation was unwelcome, so Robin took another route: buying a spare display/controller module on eBay and poking around inside it. The board turned out to be pretty complex for a coffee machine. It was built around an NXP i.MX 6 processor with an Arm Cortex-A9 core, running a Yocto-based embedded Linux system. The hardware also includes Ethernet, USB, microSD storage, and interfaces for payment hardware, cup dispensers, energy-saving modules, and more. After tracing the power circuitry and supplying the board with 24 volts, Robin got it running on the bench. events.excerpt: TL;DR A contract on Base checks every Zcash block header against Zcash’s consensus rules: the Equihash (200, 9) solution on the EIP-152 BLAKE2b precompile, the difficulty adjustment (including NU7’s 25-second blocks), the time rules and cumulative work. Contracts can then read Zcash’s best chain without trusting a bridge, a committee or whoever relays. Anyone can feed it; a feeder can delay the relay but cannot make it accept a header Zcash’s rules reject. One header costs about 626k gas (mean, whole transaction); Equihash is 361k of it. Following Zcash at 25-second blocks is ~3,456 headers, ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ gas a day: about 0.01 ETH a day at Base’s 0.005 gwei. A relay deployed with Mainnet parameters on 29 October 2026 crossed Zcash Mainnet’s NU7 activation (height 3,543,405, 6 November 2026) without a redeploy and followed the 5,405 headers after it. On top of the relay: a RISC Zero proof (Groth16-wrapped, 256,720 gas to verify on Base) that a shielded payment of at least an amount went to a receiver an app committed to, with a memo naming the app’s reference, inside the ZIP 221 chain history of a header the relay holds. The transaction id, the note, the block and the address never reach the EVM chain. A real Testnet payment was proven in 81 s on a rented RTX 4090, for about one cen
events.headline: Seam: verifying Zcash headers on Base with EIP-152, and proving shielded payments without linking the chains

Being post-quantum is not enough, we intend on being post-AI too. events.excerpt: This release brings various stability improvements, ECDSA TX-form binding, and improved replica 2.9 syncing. We recommend installing it as soon as you can to address potential node stability issues. Configuration Note: the first time you start the node after upgrading to N.2.9.8, do not use the start_from_local_state or start_from_block configuration options. Syncing: Syncing could slow down to the pace of the slowest peer, even when much faster peers were available. Each storage module limits how much sync work it keeps in progress at once. When the node reached data that only a slow peer had, that peer's requests could take up the whole limit, and the node stopped moving on to the rest of the data. The faster peers that had the rest sat idle until the slow peer was done, which could take days. Restarts made this more likely. The node kept its sync position in memory only, so after a restart every storage module started over from the beginning. If the first missing data there was only available from slow peers, the storage module synced at their pace. We reproduced both cases in the sync simulator and fixed them: A single peer can now take up at most half of a storage module's sync work limit. The node puts aside the data that peer cannot take yet and comes back to it every seco

events.excerpt: ERC-3668 (CCIP-Read) lets a contract hand a read off to a gateway, but the gateway either has to be trusted or has to return a proof the contract can verify. For many cross-chain reads a valid proof cannot be produced. That does not make the read unsafe, because the client usually already trusts its own RPC connection to the other chain and could simply make the call itself. ERC-8446 lets the client act as the gateway. The contract reverts with OffchainLookup as usual, with an x-chain URL that names the chain and contract to read, and the client calls that contract with its own RPC and passes the result to the callback exactly as eth_call returns it. No third party is involved. The chain and address are encoded as an ERC-7930 Interoperable Address, for example USDC on Base. x-chain:0x0001000002210514833589fcd6edb6e08f4c7c32d4f71b54bda02913 An optional ?finalized=true makes the read at the finalized block instead of the latest one. The client alone decides whether it can safely read a given chain, and never takes RPC endpoints from the contract. Nested x-chain lookups are not followed, so each call makes at most one cross-chain hop. Contracts can also tell when a client does not support the ERC. They add a data: URL after the x-chain URL, which only older clients reach, and it del
events.headline: ERC-8446: Cross-Chain Client Gateway for CCIP-Read

events.excerpt: ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 store metadata onchain as key-value pairs, but a JSON document has no compact way to point at those values. A URL that names the contract, the chain, and the token ID repeats what the client already knows and differs for every token. ERC-8493 defines the onchain URI scheme. The contract and token ID are not written in the URI, they come from the function that returned the document. { "image": "onchain:image/png", "thumbnail": { "small": "onchain:image/png?key=thumb.small" } } onchain:image/png is 17 bytes and works unchanged for every token. When the URI comes from tokenURI or uri , the client reads it with metadata(tokenId, key) from ERC-8048, and when it comes from contractURI , with metadata(key) from ERC-8049. A direct member of the top-level document uses its own name as the key, and everywhere else the key parameter names it. Tokens that are already deployed can use the scheme by adding a metadata_contract property to their JSON, which points the client at a separate metadata contract. Linked JSON documents keep the same contract and token, so the whole thing reads as one data tree. The scheme adds no contract surface. Existing ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 contracts support it with no change, and a client that does not know the scheme sees a URI it can ignore
events.headline: ERC-8493: Onchain URI Scheme

events.excerpt: Making your own electronics is easier than ever, but building a display from scratch is still out of reach. While hobbyists can buy LCD and OLED panels in many shapes and sizes, creating a custom display that fits an unusual surface or application requires specialized equipment and a lot of expertise. Researchers at the University of Bath have developed a new technique that could change that, making it possible to fabricate high-resolution electroluminescent displays using little more than an airbrush and a laser cutter. The technique, called Spray and Etch , combines the simplicity of spraying conductive and electroluminescent materials onto a surface with the precision of laser etching to create detailed patterns and individually addressable pixels. Unlike conventional display fabrication methods, it doesn't require expensive industrial equipment or complicated masking procedures. The process begins by spraying a thin layer of conductive copper-based ink onto a substrate. A standard, unmodified CO2 laser cutter then removes selected portions of the coating to form precisely defined electrodes. events.headline: Spray-On Displays Take Shape

Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it's needed. Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing. Gartner warned in June that the energy consumed by AI datacenters is on track to grow 26 percent this year, and grid supply may be unable to keep pace with demand by the end of this decade. Howden's analysis of data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and S&P Global found that since the year 2000, power being fed to data campuses has risen 19 percent a year on average, while the electricity grid expanded capacity by just 2 percent per annum over the same period. Datacenters' share of US grid capacity was circa five percent in 2025, up from 0.1 percent in 2000 – a 50-fold increase. events.excerpt: The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong. This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data. The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica. Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape. Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. events.headline: Scientists check their work and confirm it with update on iconic black hole image

events.excerpt: Summary LlamaRisk is building Aave’s Risk Layer: automated risk solutions that make expert risk judgment verifiable, with every parameter, bound and action checkable onchain. The Aave Risk Framework set this direction in June by making continuous risk oracles part of the protocol’s standing infrastructure. Governance and manual review can trail a fast-moving event by hours, and the evolution of AI capabilities keeps shortening the time between finding a weakness and exploiting it, so protection has to run continuously and at machine speed. LlamaGuard PT went live in September as the first of these solutions. We continue the rollout with LlamaGuard Caps as the next addition. Aave’s greatest strength is its liquidity, deep enough to move capital instantly and at scale. Defending access to that liquidity programmatically protects Aave’s users, even when a failure elsewhere in DeFi puts compromised collateral or stolen assets in play. LlamaGuard Caps hardens Aave’s perimeter. Its first stage, a borrow rate limiter for Aave V3, gives each reserve a margin of borrowing room above its debt, sized to the reserve. events.excerpt: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey. COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20. This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31. In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked. This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US.
